meta.description: Genuinely Thomas Campbell — stanza 6 of "Hallowed Ground," first printed in The New Monthly Magazine, October 1825. Published 1825, poet died 1844: unambiguously public domain and free to reuse, including on memorials and merchandise.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: It is the closing couplet of stanza 6 of ‘Hallowed Ground,’ first printed in The New Monthly Magazine in October 1825, which Campbell then edited. In the poem the lines are broken as “To live in hearts we leave behind / Is not to die”; memorial use almost always runs them together as one sentence, which is faithful enough to the sense.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: But strew his ashes to the wind Whose sword or voice has served mankind,— And is he dead, whose glorious mind Lifts thine on high?— To live in hearts we leave behind Is not to die.
trail: The line is stanza 6 of ‘Hallowed Ground,’ a poem Campbell published in The New Monthly Magazine in October 1825 while he was its editor Wikiquote ↗.
Sourcing collections cite it identically — ‘Hallowed Ground,’ st. 6 (1825) — rather than as a floating aphorism WIST Quotations ↗.

The full stanza survives intact in printed texts of the poem, where the famous line is the fifth of six lines and resolves the stanza’s question about whether a person whose mind lifts others is truly dead full poem ↗.

An autograph manuscript of ‘Hallowed Ground’ in Campbell’s own hand is catalogued by the antiquarian trade, tied to the same October 1825 magazine appearance — corroboration at manuscript level, not just reprint level.
source.excerptNote: Stanza 6 entire. The memorial one-liner takes the last two lines; read in place, they answer the stanza’s own question — ‘And is he dead, whose glorious mind lifts thine on high?’
source.rightsNote: Free to reuse without permission, including commercially. Published in 1825 and written by a poet who died in 1844, it is clear of copyright in the United States (pre-1929 publication) and in life-plus-70 jurisdictions many times over. You may reproduce the line, the stanza, or the whole poem — on a headstone, a memorial card, a product, anywhere. The only caveat is the ordinary one: a modern annotated edition’s notes and apparatus can carry their own copyright, but the verse itself does not.

author.name: Thomas Campbell
author.heading: Thomas Campbell
author.bio: Thomas Campbell (1777–1844) was a Scottish poet best known in his lifetime for The Pleasures of Hope (1799) and for patriotic songs such as ‘Ye Mariners of England.’ He edited The New Monthly Magazine in the 1820s and helped found the University of London. Today he is read far less than he is quoted: this one couplet from ‘Hallowed Ground’ has outlived nearly everything else he wrote, carried along on gravestones and funeral cards by people who have never heard his name.

misattribution.heading: Correctly credited — watch the wording
misattribution.intro: This is one of the rare memorial quotations whose attribution holds up. Campbell really wrote it, and the source is pinnable to a month and a magazine. The drift is in the text and in a common assumption about who is being remembered.

items.who: ‘To live in the hearts we leave’
items.why: Some collections print ‘To live in the hearts we leave / Is not to die!’ — adding ‘the,’ dropping ‘behind,’ and adding an exclamation mark. Treat it as a condensed rendering; the canonical line is ‘To live in hearts we leave behind.’

Campbell wrote it as two lines within a six-line stanza. Running it together as a single sentence is near-universal on headstones and cards and does no harm to the sense — but it is a reformatting, not the poem.

In the poem the subject is someone ‘whose sword or voice has served mankind’ — a public figure whose influence outlives them. Memorial use quietly widens it to anyone loved, which is a generous reading rather than a wrong one.

misattribution.truthLine: Genuinely Thomas Campbell, ‘Hallowed Ground,’ stanza 6, first printed October 1825 — and, unusually for a memorial quotation, entirely free to reuse sourced attribution ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: Campbell is making an argument, not offering a consolation. The stanza asks whether a person whose mind still lifts yours can really be called dead — and answers that continuing to live in other people’s hearts is a form of not dying at all.
It has become one of the most-carved lines in the English-speaking world precisely because it does the work a headstone needs doing in eleven words: it refuses the finality without denying the death.
